title: How to troubleshoot a failing HTTP request
description: Learn a systematic process for diagnosing failed or slow HTTP requests using browser tools, server logs, and command-line utilities.

data.text: A failed or slow HTTP request is one of the most common production incidents. The challenge is that failures can live in DNS, TCP, TLS, the application, or the client. A systematic troubleshooting process prevents random guessing and helps you reach the root cause faster.

data.title: Troubleshooting steps
items: Reproduce the issue consistently if possible.
Check the browser DevTools Network panel for status code, timing, and response body.
Identify which stage is slow: DNS, TCP/TLS, waiting (TTFB), or content download.
Verify the URL, method, headers, and request body.
Check server logs for matching timestamps and error messages.
Use curl or a similar tool to isolate the browser from the equation.
Trace network hops with traceroute or mtr if routing is suspected.
Check third-party dependencies if the request targets an external API.

data.title: Isolate the client first
data.text: Browser extensions, cached state, and service workers can all affect requests. An incognito window or a fresh curl request removes client-side variables quickly.
curl is the universal HTTP debugging tool. With the right flags, it shows DNS resolution, connection timing, TLS details, headers, and the full response.

data.title: Useful curl flags
items: -v verbose output with headers and handshake details
-w timing breakdown with connection, TLS, and total times
-I fetch headers only, no body
--trace-ascii raw HTTP bytes for deep inspection

data.title: TTFB is not always the server's fault
data.text: TTFB includes network latency and TLS time. Always compare server-side logs with client-side timings before concluding the application is slow.
When the network is the problem

items: Use traceroute or mtr to visualize routing path and packet loss.
Check if the problem is specific to a region or ISP.
Test with alternative DNS resolvers to rule out DNS issues.
Verify TLS certificates and protocol versions with openssl s_client.

data.text: When the server is the problem

items: Check application logs for exceptions and stack traces.
Verify database connection pools and query performance.
Inspect load balancer and reverse proxy health status.
Monitor CPU, memory, and disk usage on the server.
Check for dependency failures such as payment gateways or email providers.

items.text: Can I reproduce the failure in curl?
Does the issue happen across networks and devices?
Do server logs show an error at the same timestamp?
Are TLS certificates valid and unexpired?
Does a direct IP bypass work?
Is the CDN or proxy returning an error response?

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Start by isolating the client from the problem using curl or incognito mode.
Use DevTools timing columns to localize the delay to DNS, TCP, TLS, TTFB, or download.
Cross-reference client timings with server logs before assigning blame.
Have a checklist for common failure patterns to reduce mean time to resolution.
data.takeaway: Effective HTTP troubleshooting is methodical, not magical. Isolate layers, compare timings, and let evidence guide your fix.

items.question: Why does a request work in curl but fail in the browser?
items.answer: Browsers enforce CORS, cookies, extensions, and service workers. curl does none of these. If curl works, start by checking CORS headers and browser extension interference.

items.question: What is the difference between ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED and ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED?
items.answer: ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED means the host was found but no process is listening on the port. ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED means DNS failed entirely.

items.question: How do I debug a request that only fails sometimes?
items.answer: Collect timing data and error rates. Intermittent failures usually point to load balancer health checks, database timeouts, or dependency rate limits rather than deterministic code bugs.

data.text: In troubleshooting, the question is not whether the server is broken, but which layer of the stack broke first.
